The Establishment
thee es-TAB-lish-ment
noun (Boomer slang)
From establish (Old French establir, Latin stabilire, "to make firm"). For centuries the establishment meant a state church — the Church of England "by law established." The modern sense of an entrenched ruling class was popularized by the British journalist Henry Fairlie in The Spectator (September 1955), writing of the network of officials and families who really ran Britain. American students imported it in the early 1960s, and by 1967 "the Establishment" was the counterculture’s name for every grown-up institution at once: government, business, university, church, and parents.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To a Boomer of 1968, the Establishment was the whole interlocking order of power — Washington, Wall Street, the Pentagon, the dean’s office, the denomination, and Dad — that seemed to decide everything and answer to no one. The young set themselves against it, and many of them later ran it. The Christian observation begins where Scripture begins: there is an establishment, and it is God’s. "He removeth kings, and setteth up kings" (Dan 2:21); every earthly order stands only so long as He establishes it. So the believer neither worships the human establishment nor despises it. He does not worship it, because "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help" (Psa 146:3), and because the establishments of the world have often "set themselves" and taken "counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed" (Psa 2:2) — that is how the Lord of glory was crucified, by priests and governors acting together. He does not despise it, because the same God commands honor to the powers that be (Rom 13:1). And he knows how the story ends: "He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh" (Psa 2:4). The Church herself is God’s establishment in the world, built on the one foundation that no protest can shake and no committee can replace.

Webster 1828 Definition

Boomer counterculture name (from 1955 British usage) for the entrenched ruling order — government, business, university, church — which Scripture neither worships (Psa 146:3) nor despises (Rom 13:1), because God removeth and setteth up kings.

THE ESTABLISHMENT, n. (Boomer slang, 1960s; from British political usage, 1955) The dominant group of officials, institutions, and families who hold power in a society and resist change; the "system." "Don’t sell out to the Establishment."

Webster (1828) — ESTABLISHMENT, noun The act of establishing, founding, ratifying or ordaining. 1. Settlement; ; fixed state. 2. Confirmation; ratification of what has been settled or made. 3. Settled regulation; form; ordinance; system of laws; constitution of government. Bring in that establishment by which all men should be contained in duty. 4. Fixed or stated allowance for subsistence; income; salary. His excellency--might gradually lessen your establishment 5. That which is fixed or established; as a permanent military force, a fixed garrison, a local government, an agency, a factory, etc. The king has establishments to support, in the four quarters of the globe.

Older English sense: the Establishment — a church established by law, as the Church of England.

Decode for families: the Boomers who rebelled against the Establishment became it. Every generation must learn that the problem is not who sits in the chair but what sits in the heart.

Key Scripture

Dan 2:21 — "And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:"

Psa 2:2 — "The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed, saying,"

Psa 2:4 — "He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision."

Psa 146:3 — "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help."

Modern Corruption

The counterculture made the Establishment the enemy and youth the savior; Scripture teaches that God sets up and removes every establishment, and that trust in princes — old or young — is misplaced.

expand to see more

The word did two things at once. It named something real: there are networks of power, and they do protect themselves, and the Psalmist saw the kings and rulers of the earth take counsel together against the LORD (Psa 2:2). But it also built a myth: that the Establishment is the source of evil and that the young, the outsiders, and the protesters are innocent of it. History closed that myth quickly. The students who occupied the dean’s office in 1968 held the dean’s office by 1998. Power did not become pure by changing hands; it changed hands and stayed the same. "Put not your trust in princes" (Psa 146:3) includes the princes you elected yourself.

God’s way of overturning establishments is not the protest but the cross. "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty" (1Co 1:27). A carpenter’s Son, executed by the establishment of His day, rose and outlasted Rome. The Christian therefore holds every human institution loosely, honors it duly, prays for it faithfully, and laughs with the One who sits in the heavens (Psa 2:4).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin stabilire → Old French establir → English establish; 17th-c. "the Establishment" = state church → 1955 Fairlie (ruling class) → 1960s US counterculture.

expand to see more

Latin stabilis — firm, steadfast; stabilire — to make firm

Old French establir → Middle English establisshen — to set up, to settle

17th–19th c.: the Establishment — the church established by law (Church of England)

1955: Henry Fairlie, The Spectator — the informal ruling class of Britain

1960s: US counterculture — government, business, university, church, and parents together

Usage

""In ’68 your grandfather was against the Establishment; by ’88 he was on the bank board.""

"God removeth kings and setteth up kings (Dan 2:21); no establishment stands without Him."

"Honor the powers, but put not your trust in princes (Psa 146:3)."
